However, direct comparisons to human safety benchmarks are challenging due to inconsistent crash reporting standards and exposure data. This study integrates public data from the NHTSA Standing General Order (SGO), the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), and the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) to compare supervised and driverless urban ride-hailing ADS with human-driven Transportation Network Companies (TNCs) in California. Our analysis found that both aggregated supervised ADS and driverless Waymo operation had lower crash rates per million miles (CPMM) compared to human TNC drivers. Driverless ADS also showed a lower injury crash rate than the human benchmark. Furthermore, a weighted regression analysis identified that injury outcomes were correlated with crash context, such as the involvement of vulnerable road users and pre-crash movements. Data inconsistencies are impeding efforts to make direct \\\"apples-to-apples\\\" safety comparisons, highlighting the need for standardized data collection to properly assess ADS safety performance.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6216678\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.5220/0014631900004055\", \"title\": [\"Realistic Multi-Agent Path Planning in Constrained Industrial Environments Applied to New Task Execution Unit Benchmarks\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.5220/0014631900004055\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.4727525\", \"title\": [\"YOLOv8-Based Automa…
